title: The wonderful good people
hookLine: humble Shin followers remembered for their joyful faith, like the clog-maker Saichi

cards: Saichi made wooden clogs for a living, in a small seaside town in Japan. He sits at his bench shaping them, the kind with two wooden teeth underneath.
His plane pulls long pale curls of wood off the block, and they pile up on the floor. Every so often he stops, picks up a shaving, and writes a few words on it with a brush. Then back to work.
Tradition says that at the end of the day, he copied the words from the shavings into notebooks. They were poems, simple ones, and again and again they came back to the name: Namu Amida Butsu.
Today's word is what Shin Buddhists call people like him: myokonin.

teach.b: First, the word. Myokonin means wonderful good people.
Shin Buddhists use it for ordinary followers, farmers, shopkeepers, servants, craftsmen, remembered not for learning or rank but for the joy and simplicity of their entrusting.
Stories about them were collected and passed around, the way other traditions pass around stories of saints.

teach.h: A CLOG-MAKER WHO WROTE ON SHAVINGS.
teach.b: Second, Saichi himself, a clog-maker who never became a priest or a scholar.

His verses talk to Amida the way you'd talk to someone in the next room: plain, sometimes funny, and some end in the name, as if the poem ran out of words and the nembutsu took over. Later, the writer D. T.
Suzuki brought Saichi's verses to readers far beyond his town. Third, what's surprising. These aren't the verses of a man who thinks he has become good.

teach.h: HIS FAULTS AND HIS JOY, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: Saichi writes bluntly about his own faults, his craving, his temper, the ordinary mess of a person, and right beside that, the joy.
That's this week's pattern, lived at a workbench: Shinran's honesty about passions, the trust that is given rather than built, the name said in thanks. Fourth, why the tradition holds them up.

teach.h: NO MONASTERY NEEDED: SAWDUST WILL DO.
teach.b: In its telling, a myokonin shows that this path doesn't need a monastery or a library.
It can happen to a man with sawdust on his sleeves. The teaching Rennyo sent out in plain letters came back, in Saichi, written on scraps of wood.

how: Shin Buddhists tell and read stories of myokonin, humble followers known for joyful entrusting, and Saichi's simple nembutsu verses are read in Shin communities and beyond.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose goodness never made the news: a grandparent, a janitor at your old school, a neighbor who always waved, a nurse whose name you never learned.
Picture them at their ordinary work, and notice one small thing they did that you still carry. Let a silent thank-you go their way, in whatever words fit you.
